part.text: {"reframes":[{"bottleneck":"The compute axis scales molecule count (8→120) under one fixed force field, so if the error is a systematic LOPLS-AA bias, every added molecule buys the same biased estimate and the 25% floor cannot move — the plan itself labels compute 'not the lever' and then spends 59 machine-hours anyway.","assumption":"The force field is held fixed: 'one fixed force field' (LAMMPS LOPLS-AA) appears in the hypothesis and test, and the chemistry-dependence of the error is asserted but never separated from the parameterization.","reframe":"Swap the axes: fix a 16–24 molecule panel spanning hydrocarbons and esters, and spend the compute on a force-field/parameterization axis instead (2–3 off-the-shelf alternatives such as OPLS-AA and GAFF2, plus systematic LJ/torsion scaling of LOPLS). The measured quantity stays viscosity and thermal conductivity vs the same measured reference values, but each new run now tests a different error floor rather than re-sampling the same one.","question":"On a fixed 24-molecule C10–C50 hydrocarbon/ester panel, does any of 6–8 classical force-field parameterizations bring held-out viscosity mean absolute percent error (measured against the reference set's experimental viscosities) below 15%, and what is each parameterization's signed thermal-conductivity error vs the measured conductivities?","measure":"Re-run the published 8 molecules under two alternative off-the-shelf force fields with the identical 6×5 ns Green–Kubo protocol: 16 molecule-runs at the observed ~$4.50/molecule, roughly $70 and ~4.5 machine-hours, using the check-first machinery already built.","compute_after":"Each additional dollar samples a new point in force-field space with a chance of breaking the 25% floor; compute now improves an error-vs-parameterization curve instead of adding molecules at a fixed floor, and any winning parameterization can then be scaled across molecules with the original plan.","exact":"Viscosity MAPE < 15% and Spearman ρ vs measured viscosity > 0.9 on the 24-molecule panel for at least one parameterization, with per-class (hydrocarbon/ester) signed errors reported for both viscosity and thermal conductivity.","expected":"One or two parameterizations cut hydrocarbon viscosity error to roughly 12–18% while esters stay above 20%, showing the floor is parameterization- and class-dependent rather than a universal chemistry constant; thermal-conductivity over-prediction persists across all of them.","fails_if":"Every parameterization gives >25% viscosity error with the same sign pattern on the same molecules — then the floor is real for this class of fixed-charge force fields, and the molecule-scaling plan is certified as buying only more of the same.","closest_prior":"Ogbomo 2026, eight molecules under a single force field [s_ogbomo_md]; this reframe keeps that protocol and adds the parameterization axis the block never varied."},{"bottleneck":"Green–Kubo viscosity converges slowly (a collective stress autocorrelation), which is why each molecule costs 6×5 ns; most of the $940.98 buys statistical-noise reduction on an absolute quantity when the stated decision only needs a ranking of coolants.","assumption":"That the quantity measured must be the Green–Kubo viscosity and thermal conductivity themselves, and that absolute accuracy against measurement must come before ranking can be trusted.","reframe":"Change the measured quantity: compute self-diffusion coefficient D from mean-squared displacement, a single-particle average that converges roughly an order of magnitude faster than Green–Kubo stress integrals, and rank molecules by a diffusion–viscosity scaling relation (inverse D–η coupling / entropy scaling). Reserve expensive Green–Kubo for a small calibration subset that maps proxy to viscosity. A reverse-NEMD viscosity is a fallback proxy, also cheaper to converge than Green–Kubo.","question":"On the published 8 molecules, does the Spearman rank correlation between 1/D (measured from 6×1 ns MSD trajectories) and the measured experimental viscosities match, within ±0.05, the Spearman correlation of the full 6×5 ns Green–Kubo viscosity against the same measured viscosities?","measure":"Near-zero cost if the check-first trajectories are retained: re-analyze saved coordinates for MSD and D (~$0, analyst time only). If trajectories must be rerun: 8 molecules × 6 × 1 ns ≈ 48 ns, about one-fifth of the check-first run, roughly $10 and under 1 machine-hour.","compute_after":"Each additional dollar screens roughly 5–10× more molecules for the ranking objective; Green–Kubo compute is spent only on a 12–16 molecule calibration/validation subset, so the 835-molecule reference set — not 120 — becomes the reachable screen size.","exact":"Spearman ρ(proxy ranking, measured ranking) ≥ 0.9 on the 8 published molecules and on a held-out 16-molecule subset before any large proxy screen is committed; report ρ separately for hydrocarbons and esters.","expected":"D-based ranking reaches ρ ≈ 0.85–0.95 for viscosity within the homologous series but fails for thermal conductivity, which needs its own calibration and remains on the expensive protocol.","fails_if":"Proxy rank correlation < 0.8 on the 8-molecule check, or the D–η relation breaks at the hydrocarbon/ester class boundary (separate slopes per class) — then the proxy does not transfer and the original expensive protocol stands as the cheapest trustworthy ranker.","closest_prior":"Ogbomo's 8-molecule Green–Kubo ranking against measurement [s_ogbomo_md]; the reference database [s_ogbomo_db] supplies the measured viscosities used to score the proxy."},{"bottleneck":"The objective is raw per-molecule absolute error and rank correlation, so molecules are scored independently; yet the hypothesis claims the error is chemistry-dependent, i.e. structured and learnable. No pooling across chemistry classes is attempted, so more molecules buy only more uncorrected samples and the bias-correction threshold at 120 molecules is asserted, not measured.","assumption":"The unit of work is one molecule scored alone, and bias correction is a pass/fail gate applied at the end rather than the object being estimated; the objective is taken to be absolute accuracy instead of the number of calibration molecules a shared correction needs.","reframe":"Change the unit of work to a chemistry-class correction parameter and the objective to the learning curve of a class-conditional bias model (multiplicative correction per class with a chain-length slope). Compute buys calibration points at 8→16→24→48 molecules with held-out error measured at each size, and the decision question becomes how few molecules suffice to hold corrected error under threshold — a variant asks the same for a yes/no screen, refining replicas only for molecules near the decision threshold.","question":"As the calibration subset grows 8→16→24→48 molecules, does leave-group-out viscosity MAPE after a two-class (hydrocarbon vs ester) multiplicative bias correction — measured per molecule as the MD-to-measured viscosity ratio against the reference set's experimental values — fall below 15% by 24 training molecules, and are the fitted correction factors stable to ±5% between subset sizes?","measure":"First step costs ~$0: fit the two-class correction on the published 8 molecules' reported errors and leave-one-out cross-validate (analysis only). If LOO MAPE drops below ~20%, commission one 16-new-molecule tier (≈ $70, ~4.5 machine-hours) to confirm the curve direction before any 48- or 120-molecule spend.","compute_after":"Each added molecule now shrinks a shared bias model for its whole class, so held-out error falls faster than 1/√N sampling; the 48- and 120-molecule tiers are spent only if the curve has not already flattened below 15%, and boundary-adaptive replica allocation buys classification confidence where it is cheapest.","exact":"Stratified held-out viscosity MAPE < 15% at ≤24 training molecules with correction factors stable to ±5%; for the yes/no variant, ≥95% correct keep/reject calls at the coolant screening threshold with replicas concentrated within ±25% of the threshold viscosity.","expected":"The hydrocarbon correction factor is constant within ±8%, cutting held-out error to ~12–18% by 16–24 molecules; esters need 24–48; the thermal-conductivity correction is the cleanest because the published bias was same-signed for all 8 molecules.","fails_if":"Leave-one-out error on the 8-molecule fit stays ≥25%, or fitted correction factors vary by more than 50% across chain lengths within a class — then the 'chemistry-dependent floor' is per-molecule noise with no class structure, no pooled correction can beat it, and the original per-molecule scoring is the right unit after all.","closest_prior":"The hypothesis [s_ogbomo_res] asserts the chemistry-dependent floor and the published 8-molecule comparison [s_ogbomo_md] supplies the first calibration set; no bias-model learning curve is measured anywhere in the block."}]}
